faq.q: What should I journal about when I'm overthinking?
faq.a: Write about the specifics, not the summary: what exactly happened, in order, and what the next concrete step is. Match the prompt to the kind of overthinking, such as replaying the past, worrying about the future or circling a decision. Stop when nothing new is turning up on the page.

faq.q: What are good journal prompts for overthinking at night?
faq.a: If the same sentence keeps coming back, write it down once, then rewrite it starting with "I'm having the thought that..." Note any task it needs tomorrow on a separate scrap, then throw the rest of the page away. Keep it to about five minutes.

Yes, if the writing turns into rumination on paper. Warning signs are rewording the same point for ten minutes, drifting from what happened to what it says about you, and feeling worse night after night with nothing new learned. When that happens, write one next step and close the notebook.

faq.q: How do I stop overthinking a conversation?
faq.a: Write what you actually said, as close to word for word as you can, and what the other person did right afterward. Research on the spotlight effect and the liking gap suggests people overestimate how much others notice their slips and underestimate how much others liked them.

faq.q: How do I stop overthinking a decision?
faq.a: Write the decision as a yes-or-no question, list three must-haves that would make an option good enough, and ask what new information would actually change your mind. If you can't get that information this week, more thinking is unlikely to settle it.

informationGain: Unlike the top-ranking lists, which give unlinked prompts in one undifferentiated pile, this piece sorts 30 prompts by six kinds of overthinking, grounds each group in a linked study (concreteness training, worry-outcome checking, satisficing, the spotlight effect and liking gap, self-compassion, cognitive defusion), and pairs every prompt with a follow-up question so it ends instead of looping.
